analysis.one_liner: Sets mercury emission limits for coal power plants and makes those limits the only mercury standard.
analysis.headline: Introduced July 1, 2010 with zero cosponsors, the bill never left the House Energy and Commerce Committee and expired when the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require every coal-fired power plant over 25 megawatts to capture 80% of the mercury in its coal (or meet an equivalent rate) from 2012 through 2014, and 90% from 2015 onward. Plants would have to install continuous mercury monitors and pay a $50,000 penalty for every pound of mercury emitted over the limit [S2][S3]. But the bill also states that these limits would be the sole mercury standard for power plants, superseding any other Clean Air Act requirement — including the stricter, court-required EPA standards that were then in the works [S2][S3]. It died in committee without a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor [S1][S4][S5].
analysis.who_benefits: People living near or downwind of coal plants would get a real reduction in mercury — a neurotoxin that accumulates in fish and reaches the public mainly through seafood eaten by pregnant women and children. Companies selling mercury monitoring equipment and control technology would gain a guaranteed market. Coal plant operators would also gain in one way: a statutory standard they could plan around, with averaging flexibility and an escape hatch, instead of the stricter EPA rule the courts had set in motion.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Communities near coal plants and monitoring-equipment makers

how_it_helps.text: Requires coal-fired generating units over 25 megawatts to capture 80% of inlet mercury (or emit no more than 1.6 lb per trillion Btu) for 2012-2014, and 90% capture (or 0.8 lb per trillion Btu) from 2015 onward [S2][S3].
Mandates continuous emissions monitoring systems for mercury on every affected unit, with specified reference methods for calibration [S2][S3].
Imposes a $50,000 penalty per pound of mercury emitted above the annual limit, prorated by fraction of a pound [S3].

The bill's own findings cite the 2000 EPA finding that utility mercury regulation is 'appropriate and necessary' and the 2008 court decision vacating the Bush-era cap-and-trade rule, positioning the bill as the legislative response [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Owners of coal-fired power plants would pay for mercury control technology, continuous monitoring systems, and penalties for excess emissions — costs likely passed to electricity customers. At the same time, the public would give up something: by making this title the sole mercury standard, the bill would have replaced the stricter health-based EPA rules that a federal court had required, potentially locking in weaker limits than the agency would have set on its own.
analysis.who_pays_short: Coal plant owners, electricity customers, and the stricter EPA standard

drawbacks.text: The bill declares its limits the 'sole emission standard' for mercury from power plants, superseding section 112 of the Clean Air Act — meaning it would have displaced the Maximum Achievable Control Technology standards that the D.C. Circuit had ruled the EPA legally required and was then developing, which were generally stricter and health-based rather than a fixed percent capture [S3].

Owners may average emissions across multiple units at a facility or across all units they own in a state, so a dirtier plant could keep emitting if other units in the company's fleet over-comply [S3].

A plant that installs the required equipment but still misses the 2015 limit can request an 'alternate emissions limitation' from the EPA administrator — and while the request is pending, it is deemed in compliance and owes no penalty [S3].
For some plants, a $50,000-per-pound penalty could be cheaper than installing and running control technology, making payment a business choice rather than a deterrent [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would have delivered genuine, enforceable mercury reductions with real monitoring and penalties — a public health win. But its central structural feature cuts the other way: by superseding all other mercury requirements, it would have replaced the stricter, court-mandated EPA standard with a statutory ceiling on how clean power plants had to get. Weighing those, it is a real but partially self-limiting improvement — reductions the EPA was likely to require anyway, packaged with flexibility provisions the industry had sought and without the health-based stringency of the agency's own rule.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee the day it was introduced, got no cosponsors, was never scheduled for a hearing or a vote, and expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Jim Costa introduced the bill on July 1, 2010, and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day [S1][S5].
No other member cosponsored the bill [S4].
The action history shows no hearings, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action before the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011 [S5].

EPA proceeded on its own track under the Clean Air Act and finalized the Mercury and Air Toxics Standards for power plants in December 2011 — a stricter, health-based rule issued under the court-mandated process this bill would have superseded (widely reported public record).

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the court-required EPA rulemaking continued and produced stricter mercury standards for coal plants than this bill would have written into law. Coal plant operators never received the averaging flexibility and alternate-limitation escape hatch the bill offered. Nobody publicly championed the bill's defeat — it simply attracted no support and no attention.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The stricter EPA rule, over the bill's limits

for.name: Jim Costa
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Mercury Reduction and Energy Security Act on July 1, 2010; it was his sole sponsorship and attracted no cosponsors.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee leadership
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing, markup, or vote; the bill sat in committee until the Congress expired.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and no opposition is on the record; the only visible signal is that not one member of either party cosponsored the bill.

industries.note: The bill would force plants to buy mercury controls and monitoring and face $50,000-per-pound penalties, but it also gives them fleet-wide averaging, an alternate-limitation escape valve, and — most importantly — preemption of the stricter health-based EPA standard the courts required. Utilities gain predictability and weaker limits; the public gains reductions but not as much as under the EPA rule.

industries.industry: Mercury monitoring and control technology makers
industries.note: The bill mandates continuous emissions monitors and specifies approved reference methods, creating a guaranteed market for monitoring equipment and sorbent and control technology — a gain that runs alongside the public health benefit.
A 90% capture mandate keeps coal-fired generation viable under a clear federal standard rather than pushing utilities toward fuel switching, but the control costs attach to coal burning at the plant.
